speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
Noting that the United States Nuclear Regulatory Commission is changing its position almost daily over the question of nuclear plant safety, and that a freeze on new American nuclear power installations has now been imposed, I move, seconded by the hon. member for New Westminster-Coquit-lam (Miss Jewett):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
Considering that the Minister of Transport indicated in a major address in Toronto several days ago that, contrary to commitments by the previous government, he may well expand Toronto international airport, and considering that such an action will directly affect not only the environment but the actual physical and mental well-being of many thousands of people through added noise and air pollution, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Etobicoke North (Mr. MacLaren):
That this House urge the Minister of Transport to hold public hearings and release all studies on the implications of expanding Toronto international airport before proceeding with such an expansion, and that meanwhile the minister assure this House that flight curfews and landing and take-off rotations continue as agreed to by the previous government.

subtopic: THE ADMINISTRATION
THE ADMINISTRATION
subsubtopic: COMBINING OF DEPARTMENTAL PORTFOLIOS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. Yesterday, the hon. minister from Wellington-Dufferin-Simcoe in a little, staged "pas de deux" with the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra, stated that his main ministerial duty is to be in charge of SIN-social insurance numbers. He said his job is to roll back SIN. That has a nice ring to it-"the minister of state for SIN"-and it may well take all that minister's capabilities.
But how can the Prime Minister reconcile such a whimsical cabinet assignment when he continues to combine other very onerous double-departmental portfolios under single ministers, such as the Department of the Solicitor General and the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, the Department of the Secretary of State and the Department of Communications, and the Department of National Defence and the Department of Veterans Affairs? How can the Prime Minister reconcile those extraordinary contrasts in duties?

subtopic: THE ADMINISTRATION
subsubtopic: COMBINING OF DEPARTMENTAL PORTFOLIOS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of State indicated yesterday the range of responsibilities with which he is charged. We have introduced into the concept of government in Canada the idea of ministers of state to assist in departments which are either unusually complex or where there is an unusually high priority attached by this government.
Certainly, on the question of the Treasury Board in relation to achieving greater efficiency in government spending, in relation to making direct progress on deregulation, in relation to dealing with the effectiveness of governments which we believe were not sufficiently well addressed by the previous government, we have taken the decision that it would be useful to have a very strong team of ministers; and that is what we have.

subtopic: THE ADMINISTRATION
subsubtopic: COMBINING OF DEPARTMENTAL PORTFOLIOS
speechtext: Is this current structure of double-departmental portfolios to be permanent? subtopic: THE ADMINISTRATION

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, of course that is not the intention. I believe the former minister wanted to pose a serious question when he asked if I intend any ministerial changes. I do not intend any.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE
subsubtopic: ILLEGAL ACTS COMMITTED BY POLICE OFFICERS
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker. We are certainly reviewing the whole RCMP Act at the moment. We have already opened discussions with the provinces, as well, in respect of the general powers of police officers generally in the fulfilment of what might otherwise be looked upon as the normal investigatory powers of the police. But certainly, the rule of law must be paramount in this country, whether it affects the police or the average citizen, and certainly the police have to pay attention to the law in exactly the same way as does everybody else.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE
subsubtopic: ILLEGAL ACTS COMMITTED BY POLICE OFFICERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. gentleman for his reply. He knows that the whole question of police activity and political control over police activity is now within the terms of reference of the McDonald inquiry. 1 appreciate the reply the hon. gentleman gave; but is it his intention at this time to introduce the legislation which he describes prior to the McDonald inquiry submitting a report to the government?

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE
subsubtopic: ILLEGAL ACTS COMMITTED BY POLICE OFFICERS
speechtext:
Probably not, Mr. Speaker. There was some confusion earlier, which I think I conveyed to the House, as to the deadline by which the McDonald commission itself expected to have its core report before the government. There were dates being bandied about-as late as the end of 1981. The Prime Minister has since reported to the House, however, that we expect to have the main core report of the McDonald commission in our hands by June 1980.
When we are dealing with such a massive subject as the powers of the police in this country, with the consultation and the research that obviously has to be done respecting that and which is going on right now within the government, I rather expect that the recommendations and the advice from the royal commission will be in our hands in time for us to seriously consider them prior to the introduction of that legislation in the House.
However, it may be that we will have a draft bill ready for the House at about the same time, in which event I would expect it to be given first reading and then perhaps allowed to percolate over the summer so that everybody can consider it.

subtopic: PRIVILEGE

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: PRIVILEGE
speechtext:
Order. I have received three notices of privilege, and the order in which I received them is: first, the hon. member for Drummond (Mr. Pinard); secondly, the hon. member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet); and third, the hon. member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso (Mr. MacEachen). They all relate in one way or another-and I will certainly hear from the members-to a report in the Toronto The Globe and Mail and to incidents which took place in the House yesterday.
I want to say to the House in just two sentences, before hearing from the hon. members, that I read the report of yesterday's proceedings on the front page of this morning's The Globe and Mail, and there seemed to be an indication there that representations may have been made on the part of the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Baker) to me on behalf of the Social Credit party.
I should, of course, indicate that in the first place any reports which would indicate that concessions can be made by anyone else in the House respecting the question period except the Chair are quite incorrect and unfounded. Secondly, I can assure the House that the President of the Privy Council has at no time made a representation to me concerning the status of the Social Credit party in the House, except those that were made in common with the House leaders of the other two parties whom I have consulted on more than one occasion in the last two to three weeks. I wanted to put that on the record before calling on the hon. members.
[ Translation]

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as you mentioned, my question is twofold. It deals, on the one hand, with certain incidents that occurred in the House yesterday and, on the other, with an article that made the front page of The Globe and Mail this morning.
First of all, with regard to the incident that happened in the House of Commons yesterday, Mr. Speaker, you will recall that on the motion of the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Trudeau), you naturally recognized first, the Leader of the Official Opposition, then the leader of the NDP (Mr. Broadbent) and finally the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Clark). As a result of the intervention of the right hon. Prime Minister, you spontaneously deemed it timely to explain why you were about to recognize the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Roy). During the few minutes that your explanations lasted, we listened very closely, and I have absolutely no intention of criticizing your remarks at that time. On the contrary, I think they were not required and that anyway you had the discretionary power to recognize whomever you chose in the House at that time. Whether that discretionary power was used advisedly or inadvisedly, possibly it was used advisedly, poss-
November 7, 1979

ibly it was used inadvisedly, it is not for me to say. That is not what I want to do today.
As I did yesterday, Mr. Speaker, I will refrain from commenting on your remarks at that time. You will notice that after your remarks I only tried to be recognized on a point of order. I must admit that I had quite a lot of yelling to do in both official languages before finally saying simply the words which can be read at page 1010 of Hansard and which in a way constitute a motion to give the floor to the hon. member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy). I did not make any comments on your remarks. 1 was not questioning at all your decision to recognize the member for BeauCe. All I was doing as a member, Mr. Speaker, was to exercise a right provided by Standing Order 29 which reads, and I quote:
When two or more members rise to speak, Mr. Speaker calls upon the member who first rose in his place; but a motion may be made that any member who has risen "be now heard", or "do now speak", which motion shall be forthwith put without debate.
And that might certainly have made the situation more complex if my motion had been moved and accepted and if there had been a vote before 9.45 last night when some members were on their way in; perhaps my motion might have enabled one more Liberal member to take the floor on the motion introduced by the Liberal party and prevented the leader of the Social Credit Party of Canada from being recognized that day, giving us the impression that despite not being recognized in principle that party is recognized de facto in the House.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, the first part of the question of privilege I am raising now, the first point, is to know what we are to expect as members of the House in the future. I am not asking you in any way to change the decision you made yesterday, I have no right to ask you that. I am well aware of that. Anyway, there is no possible remedy to the damage done, if any. However, in future, as a member I would like to know if at any time, when 1 think a member other than the one you are recognizing should have the floor, I can use Standing Order 29 or if I am bound by the remarks and the decision you made yesterday.
I would like to know what comes first, the standing orders of the House or the interpretation given by you last night in the heat of the debate. This is the first point of my statement, Mr. Speaker. As for the second point, in order to conclude with this matter, for the record I would like to quote from Beauchesne fifth edition on page 99 of the English version and I quote citation 302, subparagraph 1:
When a motion that a member "be now heard" is defeated, it is assumed that the member originally recognized by the Speaker has the floor.
What does that mean? If the moving of such a motion is justified by the fact that somebody else has been recognized, how could 1 seek the floor other than by raising a point of order? That is the first part of my intervention.
Privilege-Mr. Pinard

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: I think I should help the hon. member for Drummond with the first part of his argument. I would hasten to add that this argument is absolutely sound. There is no other recourse than that which was open to the hon. member to try to seek the floor by way of a point of order. That is the only effective way to take advantage of Standing Order 29. Therefore, in attempting to do deal with the matter by way of a point of order, the hon. member was attempting to do it in the only way that was open to him. So everything was correct in what he tried to do yesterday.

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Therefore, the hon. member's argument today is absolutely beyond reproach. There is, however, a dilemma in our proceedings in respect to the use of Standing Order 29 in two respects. The first is that it is in opposition to our general practice to move a motion under a point of order. This is not the ordinary way of doing it.
It was not expected that I would be in this role yesterday at this particular hour and, therefore, I had not in any way advised the House. I had not expected to be making this decision at that time, although I had given the matter four weeks of thought because we have all been conscious of this problem. But in doing so, I was doing more than simply what was envisaged by Standing Order 29, which is that of choosing one member or another. I had in fact combined that step with a decision on a matter that has been troubling the House for some time, and that is the decision on the position in principle of the Social Credit party.
This matter troubled the House on the second day of this Parliament when we began an argument about whether or not the leader of that party could participate in the leaders' day debate. During a subsequent deliberation, I suggested to the House that it might want to resolve the problem directly by having it sent to a committee, which is a course of action that the House, for many reasons, has not seen fit to adopt. Therefore, the decision in some respects was returned to me, and I did not expect to be making the announcement on that matter at that particular time yesterday; but I knew that I would have to do it some time.
Having done that, it would appear to me that we would be in conflict with another practice, and that was that since I was resolving a procedural situation yesterday, to permit the use of Standing Order 29 in that way would have seemed to me to permit an appeal against the ruling that I had made, which we do not permit.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: We don't accept that nonsense.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: Order. Therefore, I indicate to the hon. member that his only recourse was the method that he tried to use yesterday, and I did not accept it in the circumstances. But he was perfectly correct in his attempt.

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext:
As I said earlier, Mr. Speaker, the second aspect of my statement refers to this article on the first page of

November 7, 1979
Privilege-Mr. Pinard
The Globe and Mail; in order to clarify my remarks, for the record I would like to quote a very short portion of this article. The interesting part is as follows:

Mr. Baker said in an interview that he made some representations to Speaker James Jerome on behalf of the Socreds because he was moved by Socred Adrien Lambert's look of genuine outrage when the five-member Quebec party recently walked out of the House in protest.
Mr. Jerome granted Mr. Roy "the generosity of the House" yesterday and allowed him to speak in the debate immediately after the other three party leaders-

Mr. Speaker, it gives me pleasure that you moved today to clarify your attitude on this most serious allegation made by a journalist on the front page of such an important paper as The Globe and Mail. I am expecting just as much from the government House leader, because since the Winters-Beaudoin incident in 1956, during the pipeline debate, and I checked the record, there has been no instance of a government leader daring to take the steps implied in the article, and which hopefully will be strongly denied by my hon. colleague, daring to set the business of the House without the presence of other members of other sides, through some sort of collusion, some back-door arrangement with the Speaker. I do not believe this has happened.
1 do not want the Canadian public to remain under the impression this might have been done, although there is an unfortunate chain of facts that, taken independently, are meaningless but that, put together, are strongly presumptive. Those facts in legal terms are serious, precise and concordant, they require a formal denial. There are five such facts, and I will state them briefly.
First, and it is important that this be put on record, there has been this summer in Drummondville, in my constituency, a meeting of 73 unsuccessful Progressive Conservative candidates from Quebec, who expressly requested that the right hon. Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Clark) not officially recognize the Social Credit Party of Canada. They must face that situation. Second, the truth for everyone who is not blind, is straightforward and is not a hypocrite, is that in the short term it is in the government's interest to enjoy in this House the support of the Social Credit Party of Canada on non-confidence motions. There can be no doubt about that.
Third, in the long term, it cannot be denied that on the other hand the disappearance from the Quebec scene of the Social Credit Party of Canada leaves the opposition field open to the Progressive Conservatives. This is another fact of life.
Fourth, we have seen over these last few days, despite an order from the House of Commons whose servant you are, sir, and as you indicated the first day, that there is now a gradual de facto recognition of the Social Credit party. All those facts together, Mr. Speaker, coupled with the way in which my intervention based on a rule that could have brought a vote before 9.45, that coud have prevented the Social Credit Party

of Canada from taking the floor, that could have antagonized the Social Credit party and perhaps influenced the vote that evening, all these facts put together leave us skeptical when we read that The Globe and Mail report I was referring to earlier, and indeed the Canadian public is led to wonder what is going on, if it is true that dealings can be made by the government leader without the presence of the House leaders from opposition parties, to prevent a government from falling or to make things easier for the government when there is a non-confidence motion.
This is serious, very serious. I am not making implications, I am simply stating facts. The solution is quite easy, Mr. Speaker. You did so very clearly in your intervention, from the start, as soon as today's question period was over. It is now for the government House leader to deny formally and unequivocally, to state that The Globe and Mail report is absolutely false, he never gave such an interview, in the interview he never made the allegations stated as his. This is essential in my view, if there is to be continuing respect for our democracy, if this institution is to be respected by all hon. members and by all the Canadian people.

speakeroldname: Hon. Walter Baker (President of the Privy Council and Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very happy that you made the representations that you did at the beginning of the question of privilege raised by the hon. member. I think that it is quite important for the operation of the House of Commons that you said what you said because it is precisely true. However, I am concerned about the implications of the remarks by the hon. member for Drummond (Mr. Pinard).
If I follow his argument that it would be forever improper for any member of this House of Commons to attend upon the Speaker of the House of Commons in order to apprise him of a difficulty he may be having as a member or, in the alternative, a sense of atmosphere that might be developing in the House of Commons over any particular matter, that is quite within the realm of any member of this House and is certainly not outside-

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: But you are the leader of the government.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext:
-the position of the House leader of the government. I have something here that I want to read that has perhaps escaped the attention of hon. members opposite. I hope my friend from Cape Breton will understand it. It is a quotation from a paper prepared by the Library of Parliament dated October 17, 1979, entitled "The Government House Leader in the Canadian House of Commons". The relevant section reads as follows:
The unsung heroes of the House are the party House leaders. Each must have a dual loyalty: to his party and to the House', according to John B. Stewart, parliamentary secretary to the government House leader between 1966-68.
As Leader of the Government in the House of Commons I wear one hat, but as leader of the House of Commons I wear a
November 7, 1979

hat that perhaps some members on the other side do not understand.
What 1 saw developing in the House of Commons as a result of your decision-which I cannot dispute and do not dispute- with respect to the striking committee was an atmosphere where a group of members of this House who regard themselves as a party, even though they are not regarded as a party anywhere else in this House of Commons, felt they were being denied certain rights that ought to flow to them, having regard to their own point of view.
What I was concerned about when I saw that was an atmosphere developing in this House of Commons where it would become an unproductive, argumentative place.

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: I am prepared to accept the word "argumentative" in the healthiest sense of the parliamentary system; but in the negative way in which it was developing, I went to you, Mr. Speaker-

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: You did?

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: Shame.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: Order, please. There is a conversation going on close to me and I did not hear what the hon. member just said. Could 1 hear that again?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: I went to you, Mr. Speaker, in your office. You will recall that I expressed concern to you about the atmosphere which I saw developing in this House of Commons.

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: Talk to the other House leaders.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: Subsequently there were meetings of representatives of parties, so I understand, where this matter was quite properly discussed in terms of the operation of this House of Commons. That occurred-

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: When?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: The date it occurred, I do not know.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext:
For the benefit of the hon. member and the record, and so that the House will know, my memory does serve me on this.
The President of Privy Council is referring to a Thursday meeting which was initiated at his suggestion on the Thursday morning prior to the House sitting at two o'clock on that afternoon. I brought into consultation the hon. member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso (Mr. MacEachen) and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) to discuss the suggestion which had been made to me on that day and which I acted upon that afternoon. I can remember it was a Thursday afternoon because the following day was the
Privilege-Mr. Pinard
Friday on which the five Social Credit members left the House. That was the extent of the consultation that had taken place and that is why 1 indicated at the beginning that there had been no representation made to me, except that which had been discussed in an open way with the other House leaders.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Thank you for clarifying that, Mr. Speaker. 1 am sorry I could not remember the date and thank you for going beyond that.
I think that is within my duty as leader of the House of Commons. I have some responsibilities with respect to that and it was in that atmosphere that it occurred.
You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that the next day, Friday, I guess because the members of the Social Credit party were not happy, they decided to walk out of this House.

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: Let them stay out.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: As a leader of the House of Commons, Mr. Speaker, no matter what other-

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: Government House leader.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext:
As the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons I was very much concerned about what I could see developing as a result of the attitude of at least one party in this House of Commons toward a particular group of members. So that the issue was made clear.
I want to tell members of the House how I regard the members who call themselves the Social Credit party in this House. I regard them in this way: they are not a party under the Senate and House of Commons Act and they are not a party as a result of a vote of this House; but Mr. Speaker, whether the members of the Liberal Party or the members of the New Democratic Party or anyone else regards them not as a party, they regard themselves as a party.

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: So?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext:
And so, sir, in their own minds they regard themselves as a party, and I recognize-so that it will be absolutely clear-that they are much more than a group of independents. They are entitled to certain courtesies and as a result of that, notwithstanding the fact that they are not a party and that there are only five of them, they have been given six positions on committees of this House of Commons.
I have expressed to you and to my colleagues in the House that I have no objection whatsoever if they are extended the courtesies that would normally apply to a party because of their particular position in this matter, and from the point of view of obtaining some form of peace with respect to the operations of this House of Commons.

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Hear, hear!

November 7, 1979
Privilege-Mr. Pinard

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: Let me just conclude by saying that I am not responsible for the attitude of the former government to any group of members in this House of Commons. I really do not care whether they agree or not with respect to my attitude to my job in this House. My own role in this House of Commons, sir-

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: You care about five but not about 112!

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: My role in this House of Commons is that even if one of the members of the Liberal party came to see me, 1 would do my best to help him, if that were the case-

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: Thanks a lot.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext:
-and all in accordance with the proprieties and appropriateness, and after consulting with my House leader colleagues. I am very pleased, Mr. Speaker, that you made it clear that there was the appropriate consultation with the representatives of the other parties with respect to that meeting which you and I had together, you in one capacity and me in another.
I frankly think that if I have a job at all in this House of Commons, it is certainly to lead the government and the House so as to ensure that we can have a recurrence of what occurred last night-that is, the victory of the government over an opposition that should not have brought a silly motion in any event.
I have another job as well, and that is as leader of the House of Commons to ensure that you, Mr. Speaker, and others connected with this House are aware of the atmosphere that prevails in this House of Commons. I frankly think that the representations made by the hon. member for Drummond are quite frivolous and I am sorry he made them.

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: Deny it.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: In addition, I have notice from the hon. member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) and from the opposition House leader, the hon. member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso (Mr. MacEachen). I do not know whether they touch the same subject. I would like some guidance as to the most orderly way in which to receive all of the representations. Having heard those who have given me notice, I think then I might hear any others who wish to participate and pursue the question of privilege before making any kind of a decision.

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Cape Breton Highlands-Canso):
speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have listened to really one of the most incredible performances ever given in the House of Commons. The hon. member for Drummond (Mr. Pinard) raised a question of privilege based upon an article in The Globe and Mail which stated that the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Baker) had made representations to your Honour. The article said he had waited upon your Honour. Then the article said he had made that approach because he was moved by the look of

genuine outrage on the face of one of the members of the Social Credit group. Then, lo and behold, there developed what he described as generous treatment of the Social Credit party in the House of Commons. That is the gist of the article. The hon. gentleman has confirmed in his statement that the article is correct. There is no explanation either from the hon. gentleman that later on, after he had had his private meeting with your Honour, other House leaders were called in.
I have been leader of the government in the House of Commons for quite a long time in the past, and never to this day have I called upon the present Speaker or the former Speaker, Mr. Lamoureux, in order to express my views as to what was going on in the House. Never.

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: I must say I often felt like it, but I never did because i understood the consequences of that particular kind of activity-

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: -that a member of the government, with the authority of the government, waits upon the Speaker with respect to what the hon. gentleman described as the maintenance of peace in the House of Commons. Whose peace?

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext:
I hope the House does not forget the kind of atmosphere that prevailed in the House of Commons when I was a new member when a member of the government in the midst of a crisis in the House waited upon the Speaker.
There has been an impending crisis in the House of Commons and in the midst of it we are told that the President of the Privy Council has waited upon Your Honour. You have told us, and we accept your word, that representations did not influence your conduct in any way. But I object very much indeed that the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons would go privately to Your Honour and speak about matters relating to the operation of the House of Commons.

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: Resign.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext:
It is very serious. 1 confirm what Your Honour said, that you called others, my distinguished colleague from Winnipeg, myself and the President of the Privy Council, to discuss matters; but I do not recall that I was ever informed that that meeting had been preceded by a meeting with the President of the Privy Council. I may have been, but I do not recall. So I say to the President of the Privy Council that I intend to have more to say about it, because events occurred in the House of Commons, as my hon. friend said, which drawn together cast great skepticism upon the operations of the chamber.
Why was the member for Drummond not permitted to put his motion, which might have changed the whole course of events yesterday? Your Honour has given us a statement, and
November 7, 1979

we accept it. Nevertheless, the question will linger in our minds. However, we have an even deeper question about the motives and conduct of the President of the Privy Council. I have had good relations with him but I am deeply regretful that he went to the Speaker privately.

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: Shame!

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: Unbelievable.

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question of privilege is also in two parts. First of all, I find quite unacceptable that in our parliamentary system the integrity of the Chair can be brought under suspicion as irrespectfully and as irresponsibly even, as the government leader did in his statements to The Globe and Mail reporter. This is the first part of my question of privilege.
This is even more unacceptable since we have just heard the leader of the government in the House explain his position in this matter. He was interrupted by you, Mr. Speaker, when you noted that the representations that he made privately to you occurred on a Thursday, the day before the five Social Credit members left the House in such a-

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: Dramatic manner!

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext:
-dramatic manner, as someone has just said. If this is true, I am much more willing to believe the Speaker of this House than the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker). If it is true that he waited on you privately before the five Social Credit members left the House, then The Globe and Mail article is inaccurate since it states that Mr. Baker came to you because he was moved by the look of genuine outrage on the face of the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) as he was leaving the House of Commons.
Mr. Speaker, either there has been another meeting of which we are not aware or else the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton deluded the members of the Social Credit into thinking that he would ask you to grant them a better treatment in the House to win the vote last evening.
Mr. Speaker, some facts have to be recalled in this House. As the government House leader spoke for a long time let me say this.
The difficulties of the Social Credit Party of Canada in gaining recognition in this House since the beginning of the session were created in the first place by the government leader himself. On opening day it was the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) who rose to propose the names of hon. members who would form the striking committee of this House. Yet, he was the one who decided not to include a representative of the Social Credit Party of Canada.
Privilege-Mr. Pinard
He was the one who decided before anyone else in this House that the Social Credit party should not obtain official recognition as a party in the House of Commons. He was the one who decided not to allow this political group to be represented on the striking committee of this House. It was even his leader who went and raided the ranks of the Social Credit party to convince the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Janelle) to join the Progressive Conservatives, thereby reducing by that much the representation of the Social Credit Party of Canada in this House. Obviously, Mr. Speaker, yesterday the government leader had a lot to be forgiven by the Social Crediters. I do not know what happened.
I do not know what was arranged behind the curtains of this House but I do know that in today's edition of The Globe and Mail it is reported that Mr. Baker said in an interview that he had made representations to you to get a better treatment for the Social Credit Party of Canada. I believe that the office of Speaker of this House must remain completely objective and above those kinds of influences and deals which can only tarnish the good reputation of Parliament. I am prepared to take your word, Mr. Speaker. I am prepared to accept what you said earlier but I am really puzzled by the remarks just made by the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton who, contrary to his customary eloquence and self-confidence, was today stuttering, imprecise and anxious to hide something from us. 1 wish, in the spirit of sincerity, honesty and co-operation with yourself, Mr. Speaker, he would tell us everything that happened and clearly specify not in an evasive way as he did, but clearly state what he did in an attempt to have the Social Crediters vote with the government to defeat last night's motion.
In fact, Mr. Speaker, my question of privilege is a fundamental one because we believe at this time that the government House leader used you to hoodwink the Social Crediters, that he has deceived that political party and won a vote last night that he should normally have lost.
The second part of my question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, relates precisely to what you said yourself yesterday as reported on page 1009 of Hansard, which I think was to the point and should be the element to be remembered from everything that has taken place these last few days concerning the Social Credit Party of Canada. You said that it seems that the Social Credit members should be allowed to participate as they are entitled to, since they are members of a political party and also because they form a group in the House, that they are five members all seated together in the House, and that they chose a leader, first, you said, so long as it does not give them an advantage that they would not otherwise enjoy as five members and, second, so long as it does not deprive other members of their right to participate in some way.
My question of privilege is the following, Mr. Speaker. I would have liked to take part in the debate yesterday. The House had before it a motion presented by the official opposition. It was, according to our rules, an opposition day, in fact

I think that you spoke wisely yesterday when you talked about the right to recognize, sometimes, a member-

I accept the correction of the Speaker. If we refer to what happened last night we see that in fact the hon. member for Annapolis Valley-Hants (Mr. Nowlan) intervened in the debate with a long question that took up part of the time which should normally have been allotted the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Janelle). In any event, it is essential, Mr. Speaker, that you keep in mind that the five hon. members who are called the Social Credit Party of Canada have chosen a leader as they had the right to do, but that there is also a political reality that is supreme, Mr. Speaker, that stands way above all the rules we may adopt here in this House of Commons, and that is that the people of Canada had the opportunity to decide, at the time of our recently held election, that the Social Credit party presented candidates, and that the people having expressed its will, denied that party the 12 members who would have allowed the so-called leader to receive the additional salary as leader of a party. Attempts have been made to build a case for the Social Credit Party of
Canada and give it a special place in this House because its history goes back quite some time.
Mr. Speaker, I feel it is important to recall that in the days of Mr. Thompson and Mr. Caouette, the Social Credit party was truly a national party with candidates in several provinces of Canada. Since the waning political party led by the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Roy) was not even in a position to run candidates in every Quebec constituency and had no candidate in any other Canadian province, therefore it is neither a national party nor the group led by Mr. Caouette or Mr. Thompson, but it has become a small regional party which has some rights and privileges. We on this side do not intend to deny to those democratically elected members the right to take part in the proceedings of the House, the right to speak here, the right to uphold the interests of their electors who trusted them.
However, I think that you rightly stated yesterday Mr. Speaker that rights and privileges should not be granted to that small party. I knew what I said when a while ago I used the word "waning" because this party is fading away. Mr. Speaker, it should not be granted rights that will unduly reduce the rights and privileges which with good reason belong to the loyal opposition in the House. I think that in the future, on opposition days, either those of the Liberal party which constitutes the official opposition or those of the New Democratic Party which ran candidates in all provinces and is truly a national party which may speak in the House, as I said, on those opposition days of the Liberal Party or the NDP, Mr. Speaker, you should not recognize each time a member from the Social Credit Party of Canada. Otherwise you would infringe upon those rights and privileges that the Liberal party and the NDP were given by Canadian voters during the last election, on May 22. If the Social Crediters want to have more rights in the House they should try to have more members elected. Only then shall we respect them for what they will rightly be but not until such time.

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for quite awhile I was determined to sit this one out, but things have been said, particularly about Your Honour, which make me feel I must say a few words.
Before I come to the main point that brings me to my feet, namely the reference to Your Honour, I should like to say a few words about the situation with respect to the position of the Social Credit party in this House. It has been a difficult one, and whatever may have been said or done on the floor or at meetings among House leaders, it is my conviction that Your Honour from the chair has been doing your best to straighten the matter out in terms of fairness and in terms of generosity, the word you used yesterday.

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext:
The record is quite clear that when I spoke on October 9 on the motion for setting up the striking committee

November 7, 1979

my position was, if anything, a bit severe. I was concerned, as were all my colleagues, over the possibility that immediate and wholesale recognition of the Social Credit group as a party could have a bearing particularly on the question period, as a result of which we would suffer. We believed we might lose some of the rights we felt we had earned by the increased numbers returned to Parliament to sit in this corner of the Chamber.
I have been looking over what I said that day and I find nothing wrong with it, nothing that needs to be corrected. The debate and the vote that day solved the problem in part, making it clear that the Social Credit group is a small party and that certain things which they might claim, they do not necessarily need to have. But it did not solve the whole problem. The matter of their rights in the question period, the matter of their order in debate together with a few other considerations were left to the Chair, and I find that in my remarks I made a plea that that be the case.
I felt yesterday that Your Honour's submission was an excellent one. You pointed out that what has to be considered is just simple arithmetic. 1 believe there is far too much discussion around the words "status" and "recognition". Those words have no real meaning. The Liberals are recognized as having the status of a party in this House. We are also recognized as having the status of a party in this House, but that does not give us the same rights the Liberals have. It does not allow us the number of questions in the question period the Liberals are allowed, and there are many other things where we have to take second place because we are 26 as opposed to their 112. There are remarks from the back which I hope are on the record as to the kind of opposition party we are, but that is irrelevant to this debate.
My point is that, in my view, Your Honour was quite correct yesterday in saying that from the chair you have to look at the arithmetic of the situation and that you have faced the fact that the Social Credit members in this House call themselves Social Crediters, are a party and have a leader. If there are rights to individuals and to minorities, I think all minority parties, including the Liberals, should be recognizing those rights. 1 am prepared to leave in your hands, sir, the protection of the rights of all members of this House whether on the government side, in the official opposition, in our corner or in the corner opposite.
I do not like some of the suggestions which have been made, particularly by the last speaker, which seem to be that we should take that right away from Your Honour. In my view you have had a difficult task in handling this situation during this last month, but I think that instead of your being criticized, you should be commended.

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext:
I suspect that the problem of this relationship will last as long as this Parliament lasts, but in the meantime I contend that we should pay attention to, and perhaps even
Privilege-Mr. Pinard
read again, the words of Your Honour yesterday when you ruled on the question of the spot in the day when you would see and hear the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Roy).
However, I am not sure even yet that I would have taken the time of the House to make these remarks were it not for the fact that I felt that other things which have been said today made it necessary for me to get to my feet. I know from experience, and most members of this House know from experience or from their reading of history, that the integrity of the Chair and the respect of all members for the Chair is a basic sine qua non to the operation of this House.

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext:
I do not like the suggestion that in one way or another you, sir, have been involved in some conspiracy or some arrangement somehow connected with how members would vote on a certain motion. My friends to my right do not like it, but they have come awfully close in what they have said today to impugning the Chair. I do not believe that should be done unless there is a case for it and one is prepared to go all the way. I know of one such occasion. I participated in the debate when there was a motion to criticize the Chair, and that Parliament was one of the sorry ones in the history of this country. Let us not get anywhere near that sort of thing.
Because my name has been mentioned two or three times, I want to give what evidence I can about the situation. I do not know everybody's conversation with everybody else, but I know that Your Honour called me one morning and told me that you would like me, with others, to come to a meeting in your chambers. In that telephone conversation Your Honour indicated quite openly and without any question that the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Baker) had expressed concern to you about the mood of the House because of the Social Credit situation and that you had made a decision as to what you were going to do. I believed you then, and I believe you now. You called us in and told us that you had decided that the Social Crediters were entitled to roughly three questions a week in the question period and that you planned that day to call on the hon. member for Beauce for a question during the first round. You wanted to let us know. You made it clear that you were not asking for us to confirm your decision. You were not consulting us; you were letting us know.

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: Was Allan there?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, now that you have raised the point, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has said that he received a telephone call from you telling him what had taken place earlier or later. I want to make it clear that I received no such telephone call.

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE

I am not concerned about protecting the reputation of the President of the Privy Council; he can look after himself. But I am concerned, for the sake of this House, about the reputation of the Chair. If I had thought at that point that there was any suggestion of a kind of governmental pressure being put on the Chair and that the Chair was paying any attention to it, I can assure you, sir, that I would have given you some avuncular advice. However, 1 certainly did not feel it to be necessary, and my feeling throughout the whole piece is that you have tried to handle the matter on your own as fairly and honestly as you could.
You Honour may have made some mistakes. You have already admitted that you may have made a mistake yesterday in not letting the hon. member for Drummond put his motion under Standing Order 29. We can discuss that back and forth. We can discuss the question of how we are going to get along in the House as long as this Parliament lasts. But one thing I do not want this Parliament to do is question the honesty or the integrity of the Chair unless there is absolute evidence, in which case we go the whole way.
The Globe and Mail can make its assertions. An editorial writer from another newspaper in another city telephoned me this morning. 1 suppose he had read The Globe and Mail and he asked me whether I thought it was true. Over the telephone 1 said categorically that 1 was convinced that it was not true.

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: It is not for you to defend the President of Privy Council, and that is waht you are doing.

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: Not at all. Apparently there is no denial of the fact that the President of Privy Council talked with Your Honour, but the point I want to make is that I am satisfied from Your Honour's reporting to me about that conversation that it was not a case of governmental influence or governmental pressure on the Chair. That I regard as completely out of court, and I think the President of Privy Council may have made a mistake in going to Your Honour on his own.

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: Of course he did.

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: It might have been better had he asked Your Honour to call a meeting of all of us. I said a moment ago that it might have been a mistake, and now I will say it was a mistake. My main concern is that this House have respect for the Chair, that there be no question about the integrity of the Chair, and I insist that any suggestion that the Chair was involved in how certain members would vote last night or that the Chair has been doing things at the bidding of the government is not fair to the Chair or to this House of Commons.

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Order, please. I think it might be appropriate for me to intervene very briefly here. With respect to the article in The Globe and Mail, I attempted to point out to the House early in these discussions that there was an aspect of that report in the newspaper which had to be incorrect because it seemed to me to indicate that if the President of Privy Council had made a representation, he made it as a result of the look on the faces of the Creditistes when they left the House. In fact, I pointed out to the House that the only thing which could have been interpreted, in my opinion, as any such representation by the President of Privy Council was on the day before that took place.
The second thing is that if that is to be interpreted as a representation, then I think we are setting on our course of conduct here a set of scruples which we may have to observe. However, my recollection is simply this. On that day the President of Privy Council had a suggestion to make to me, as has happened on several occasions not just by him but by other members of the House of Commons. The tone of the suggestion was very much: I have a suggestion to make for your consideration. Is it worth discussing with the other House leaders? That is as regular as clockwork in this building.
In turn, before coming into the chamber on that day and in fact recognizing one of the members of that party, I spoke with the other two House leaders and said: This has been suggested to me. What do you think of it? That was only one of several discussions which we had subsequent to that concerning what to do about this particular situation. Also I may say that I had several deputations, single, double and triple, from members of the Social Credit party who came to me to plead their case. There was nothing extraordinary about that. They indicated that they were fighting for more than simply a question or two; it was a matter of principle that they had set and so on. There was nothing irregular in any event, and I do not think any of it is a surprise to the House.
I want to set the record straight. It may have been, in the most scrupulous of standards, a mistake, as has been said, for the President of Privy Council to have done this, but I never considered it to be a representation. It was a suggestion that was made to me. The tone of it was ordinary, that I would take it up with the other two House leaders, which I did. It may very well be that that kind of conversation with one member ought never to take place. If that is the case, certainly
November 7, 1979

I am prepared to follow that standard of conduct. But it eliminates something which I have done on a regular basis for five years with all kinds of senior and junior members of this House who have, in the corridor here, or on other occasions, simply put a question to me.
I put a case in point. A new member of the House of Commons, a day or two after the original vote, spoke to me to ask about whether the vote had the significance the House had attached to it. We discussed it.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: But there is a difference.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext:
There is a difference, I grant, but if there is any suggestion that a representation to me carries with it some later pressure from the government, of course that would be something I and the House would reject out of hand.
I accept in all seriousness the point raised by the hon. members who are here today. I want to assure the House-and 1 think the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has said so-that at that time the discussion was very brief: a minute or a minute and a half, almost passing in the corridor. A suggestion, it seemed to me, was being put forward for discussion with the other House leaders. There was no suggestion of anything other than that. I am sure my response was that I would, in turn, take it up with the other House leaders, and I did.
I do not want to appear to be rushing to the defence of the President of Privy Council any more than the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre does. But at the same time 1 want to say that I did not take this suggestion at the time it was made, as anything more than a brief suggestion. My immediate reaction was to say that I would take it up with the other House leaders, which I did. It was a suggestion we have discussed several times since that time.
Furthermore, I want to conclude by saying that not since that day more than two weeks ago-and during which time I have tried to decide how to deal with the Social Credit party during question period-has the President of Privy Council spoken a single word to me about the status of the Social Credit party in the House.

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: Contrary to the report in The Globe and Mail.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: Contrary entirely to the report in The Globe and Mail.

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: Which he did not deny.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext:
All right, but I only put the record straight. 1 understand entirely that the members who raised this point exercised two or three things: first, it would appear in the content of the article that there is more than a suggestion; there is a statement in the article that in fact the President of Privy Council took responsibility for offering participation in question period. It is something he does not have to offer. That is under the control only of the Chair. The second error is that which I have pointed out to the House. The third touches a position of a political party in the House upon which the
Privilege-Mr. Pinard
members have been outspoken. I recognize that is a very serious point. The fourth relates to the matter which was very discretionary and upon which I confess a very strict interpretation of the rules was applied against the hon. member for Drummond last night.
I think the point is very serious; it needed airing and it needed exposure. I hope the House has benefited from it. If it is necessary to be super scrupulous in the future in terms of conversations with the House leaders, that can be done. But I hope that it will not eliminate forever and a day the time that a House leader may express to me a suggestion which I might take up with other parties of the House.

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are only two points I should like to make, but first of all l should like to assure you that nobody on this side criticized you or questioned your integrity and honesty.
Mr. Speaker, we have the greatest respect not only for your duties but also for your person. We have known Your Honour for quite some time and nobody criticize or even tried to criticize your decision.
The two points I should like to make are these: first, the hon. member for Drummond (Mr. Pinard) has dared the President of Privy Council (Mr. Baker) to tells us that the article published by The Globe and Mail is false as regards not only the facts, but also the motives it attributes to him.

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: He refused.

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: But, Mr. Speaker, when we talk about these motives, they might very well be motives unknown to you. It is quite possible that some discussions are going on outside the House, some negotiations you know nothing about. We have nothing whatsoever against the fact that you, as Speaker of the House, agree to discuss with a member, be it a minister, the House leader of the government or a new member. Indeed you have always done that and we want you to continue doing that. Mr. Speaker, contrary to what the member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) said a moment ago, nobody criticized your decision or doubted your integrity. The member for Drummond never talked about a conspiracy involving the Chair and the government. What he said was that there is a series of facts and that from them some persons could draw conclusions and that we want to clarify the situation. But what we note this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, is not that you have not correctly answered the question, you have, and it never crossed our minds that you had been influenced by the President of Privy Council, the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton. What we do note is that he did not have the courage to deny-

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: He is afraid.

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext:
-to take up the hon. member for Drummond's challenge to deny the intentions that The Globe and Mail

November 7, 1979
Privilege-Mr. Pinard
report attributed to him. What we take exception to, Mr. Speaker, as I have said, is not that you agreed to see him, but that he probably tried to negotiate with a group from this House in order to get their support, that he decided to act in this way, as government leader, with all the power and weight that supposes, because we must realize that it is the government which is in effect responsible for what goes on in the House.
Mr. Speaker, it was the President of Privy Council, a member of Parliament and a senior government minister who decided to try to see you with the hope of perhaps getting the support of another group. subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE

Mr. Speaker, following the question of privilege that has just been raised, I do not wish to rub it in. As we always say: in front of wolves, one has to howl with the pack. And I will honestly admit that this afternoon, I was rather afraid that your brothers of yesterday would devour you because you refused to howl along with them. It breaks their heart that we should be recognized in the House. I would now like to tell the public that it is not up to political parties in the House, not up to our opponents to decide whether or not we are entitled to speak, whether or not we are entitled to sit here, because our electors have decided that themselves.
So I would not want to dwell any longer on this, Mr. Speaker. In his remarks a while ago, the hon. member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) took it upon himself to comment on last night's vote. I regret that very much, but it is definitely not very distinguished and not very sincere to comment on the vote by one of our colleagues in the House. Perhaps in the heat of the debate the hon. member wanted to imply that the decision had influenced our vote yesterday. I would ask him simply to withdraw his words because this is not the case. We simply voted against a motion that did not make sense, a hypocritical motion, a motion that was introduced only for politicking purposes. So I would ask the hon. member kindly to withdraw his remarks. If he is a man, he is going to withdraw.
I never insinuated things like the ones he mentioned this afternoon.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: The hon. member for Papineau.

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Rimouski is asking me to withdraw remarks I cannot withdraw because I did not make them. He undoubtedly misunderstood my intervention. I brought to your attention the fact that on an opposition day assigned to the Liberal party, the official opposition in this House, four Liberal members out of 112-or 113, if we include you-Liberal members elected to the Parliament of Canada were recognized whereas by recognizing two members of the New Democratic Party and one member of the Social Credit Party of Canada, three members who in the end hold only 31 seats in this House got a representation in that debate that is not proportionate to what they should have had.

I know that earlier the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), the great expert on procedure, referred to mathematical considerations. He reminded you that the way we should treat members of the Social Credit Party of Canada from now on is not as if they were a recognized political formation. There are many dangers in attempting to adjust the minority here because mathematics do not always fit. You cannot adjust participation with scientific precision. The number five does not always divide into the other numbers in the House. For example, three members of the Social Credit party-and incidentally this is an event which went almost unnoticed-participated in the throne speech debate. If you try to apply a mathematical formula, the Social Credit members began in the very first debate with far more representation than they were entitled to as a group of five. I think we have to recognize that no matter how they are described or thought of in the minds of members, either inside of the House or outside of it, they are still entitled to some participation. My only intervention was to give them that participation to which they are entitled, and in a way that recognizes their position as a party and nothing more.

For our part, Mr. Speaker, we would far rather trust you with our rights as a minority in this House than we would the Liberal party, either in this House or outside of it.

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
