subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext:
I do not trust members on the opposite side either.
I am saying that you are the one whom we trust.
The second question raised is a fundamental one. It was raised by the hon. member for Cape Breton Highiands-Canso (Mr. MacEachen), a member everyone holds in the highest regard in this House. It concerns the relationship among House leaders of the parties and yourself, Mr. Speaker. Your Honour raised this question when you participated in the earlier round of discussion. The President of Privy Council said he thought that he had the right, indeed the obligation, as leader of the whole House-if I understood him correctly-to speak and make representations to you concerning what he felt were problems that might arise in the course of the proceedings of this House.
I am a new member and I am certainly not a member of any experience.

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: That is true.

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext:
That is fine, but we all have a right to speak, a right to listen and a right to be heard. I would suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that one example which you might follow is the practice of judges meeting counsel in chambers. From your own experience you will know that no judge would meet a counsel in chambers alone. There is always a danger that a situation could arise where something might be said or suggested which could influence a decision of a judicial nature, not simply of a political nature.

With respect, I think your function in the House in recognizing members, attempting to allocate questions and attempting to be fair is a judicial function and not a political one. I am not making an unqualified recommendation because I recognize that what I say may have some holes in it that I have not yet seen, but it seems to me that the President of Privy Council may want to consider whether, when he goes to the Speaker of the House of Commons, he is not simply going there as the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton-and he knows this-or as the President of Privy Council, but as an active member of a government party.

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: That is the point.

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: The hon. member for Cape Breton Highiands-Canso was absolutely right in saying that we were in a delicate situation yesterday. The question of recognition and the right to be recognized could have affected the outcome of last night's vote; there is no question of that. I suggest that one thing you might want to consider, Mr. Speaker, is-

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: A committee.

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext:
-not a committee but a recommendation that discussions between House leaders should not take place without all of them being present. No House leader should feel that he can make a representation of a judicial nature rather than a political nature to the Speaker of the House of Commons in exercising his judicial functions.
We have had experience of phone calls to judges. We have had experience with other attempts, with the best of will and the best of intention, to make representations of a legal nature to somebody in a judicial capacity. That has been the subject of criticism, and quite worthy criticism. We now have rules of conduct and so on for members of Parliament. All of us recognize there are things we cannot do.
I suggest to the President of Privy Council (Mr. Baker) and to the other House leaders that it may be necessary in the future for House leaders to meet with you, Mr. Speaker, in considering matters of a judicial nature, and that representations, however well intentioned-and I certainly do not question the good intentions of the President of Privy Council-should not be made privately.
I myself have made representations to you, Mr. Speaker, on a couple of matters, one of which is still outstanding, of a private nature. As members of Parliament, I think we are all entitled to raise these questions of concern. This is different. I am speaking here as a private member of Parliament to you about a private matter affecting, in this case, my conscience. I am suggesting that when the President of Privy Council is making a representation to you that is not on a private matter of conscience, that is not a private matter affecting his personal privileges as a member of Parliament, that he not make that representation without the other House leaders being present.
I think that would solve a potentially difficult problem.
November 7, 1979

The President of Privy Council raised as a comparison the relationship that existed between the president of the privy council at that time, the hon. member for Cape Breton High-lands-Canso, and my House leader in another Parliament. The difference with that experience was, of course, that the Speaker of the House of Commons was not involved in any way. That is a very significant difference.
There will, of course, be discussions and negotiations in a minority Parliament. We are grown up and recognize that these votes do not take place without prior discussion. However, there is a very real distinction between those kinds of negotiations and a discussion involving recognition, the status and position in debate of a party which is also involved, as is well known, in a political discussion with the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) and the President of Privy Council concerning a non-confidence motion. There is clearly a distinction between those two things.
Where there is a judicial function being performed, that should not be done without everyone being present. The Speaker should in no way be involved in political discussions, and that is where I leave it.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext:
To get back to an earlier point in reference to the intervention just made by the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood (Mr. Rae), we are all aware of the wisdom of the suggestion he has just made. The difficulty is that functionally it eliminates most of the contact and conversations that take place in the House. For example, several times upon a decision by the Chair a member of an individual party who has been adversely affected by that decision of the Chair will show up and say, "Are you sure you thought of this?" That is a courtesy call. I do not think the member is trying to reopen the question. The member is coming in to say that he did not quite understand my point on this. He is obviously dejected and disappointed. I could at that point say, "Look, it is not proper for me to discuss this unless we have present members of other parties".
Similarly, we get into the same situation if after a given question period a House leader comes into my office and says, "Look, our people are not happy with the number of questions". 1 must say, "Stop right there, I have to call in the other House leaders to discuss things of this sort". These are plain representations about business that is going on in the House.
I think we can follow the structures of court practice, as the hon. member has said. The only trouble is that it will put us in a formal structure that will make it less pleasant to do the business of the House. I think trust is much more useful.

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would first like to say it hardly requires any evidence to realize that we all deeply respect the position of the Speaker of the House and of the person of the Speaker himself. I feel it is rather sad that things should become so convoluted that in the course of this discussion it has been perhaps misunderstood that many of those who have stood up, in my party at least, to express their concern stood up in order to express the very deep concern that the Speaker of the House, both in his office and
Privilege-Mr. Pinard
in his person, should not be involved, should not be impugned and should not have any light cast upon him except the highest respect which this House holds for him.
Therefore, it is particularly tragic and unfortunate when we are raising a question which is not at all directed at the Speaker but in fact is directed at the very direction of the Speaker's name-the protection of the honour of this House of Parliament-that this should be misunderstood. Perhaps there were things that were said incorrectly or which were misunderstood because they were not put well, but certainly that was not the intention, so far as I have any knowledge of it, of my colleagues. What is at stake, and this is important, is that we did not ever mention the name of the Speaker of the House of Commons. We did not bring it into the press. We did not involve the name of the Speaker in terms of events that occurred last night. It is precisely because we did not that the question arises, who did?
It is this kind of thing we are concerned about. We are simply seeking to have it made clear that the people of Canada will lose respect for the parliamentary system about which we have heard so much idealistic speaking in the Speech from the Throne and so on, that that very respect which we all want to establish may in fact be put under suspicion.
Therefore, when an article appears in The Globe and Mail that seems to link a statement by some member of the House of Commons which might involve or is alleged to have involved the idea that he said he had some influence with the Speaker, it endangers the position of the Speaker.
It is this about which we are speaking, not about the Speaker himself. This is what is at stake. We were expecting, and hoped it would be said, that it would be made clear by the President of Privy Council through The Globe and Mail or anyone else that he does not intend or want to influence the Speaker, that he was sorry if it was misprinted and said in this way so as to imply that he had done such a thing, that indeed he has no intention of trying to give the impression that he gets credit for having achieved something with the Speaker of the House.
That is what is at stake. It is not the Speaker of the House who is at stake but in fact his good name. It is not that it took place at all but that people have the idea that it took place. It is not what happened, but what is perceived to have happened, that is at stake. It is this which we wish to have clarification of.
It would be very simple to say not "if 1 have" but simply that it appears that my involvement of the word "Speaker" in this conversation with The Globe and Mail has led to this misunderstanding, one which has taken up the whole afternoon of this House. It is simply that we all, everyone in this House, want to protect the sanctity and the position of the Speaker in whom we all have trust.

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has been very seldom in the career I have had in

November 7, 1979
Privilege-Mr. Pinard
this House of Commons that 1 have taken part in a question as substantial as this. Not being a lawyer or an expert on parliamentary rules and procedure, I have usually left this to some of my more learned colleagues. However, there is something 1 would like you to help me, a private member of this House, clear up.
1 do not think anyone in this debate this afternoon has mentioned that they doubted Your Honour's word. Rather, it has been directly the opposite, that we are fighting to protect the integrity of the Speaker of the House of Commons.
I have not had time to consult my colleagues, but I have no objection if the House leader of the New Democratic Party wishes to consult you on matters that affect the interventions of his members in this House of Commons. I have no objection of any kind to that.

If the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Roy) wants to phone or write to you, Mr. Speaker, and asks to see you in your chambers here, in the House of Commons, of his own initiative, for his group, regardless of its status or non status as an official party, if he wants to speak on behalf of the group he represents in the House-
The government House leader, holds a very responsible position in this House, and I think he will agree that 1 have shown respect to him and to the office he holds, or to any other government minister whether I be in opposition or on the government side of the House. Why should the government House leader-this is the fundamental, bottom line of the question-go to you, sir, on his own placing you, inadvertently perhaps, in a position that is very precarious? Why should he take it upon himself to speak for the members of the Social Credit party, officially or not? They are very articulate people. Anybody who has seen that party operate in the House of Commons must agree that even though they are only five they are very articulate and can handle themselves very well when it comes to speaking to anyone, whether in this chamber or to you in your chambers. Why is this sudden protective umbrella held up by the government House leader?
I repeat, 1 think this is a fundamental question. If the House leader of the official opposition makes an appointment with you to discuss our interventions in this House, our rights and privileges in this House as the official opposition, that is one thing. If the government House leader does the same on behalf of his party, I see no objection to that. But why should he all of a sudden appoint himself an officer to protect the rights of a five-member group who are well known for their ability to get up and speak and look after themselves?
I suggest this would change the complete atmosphere of this House. I repeat, with all due respect to the government House leader, that this argument could be over in five minutes or five seconds: all he has to do is stand in his place and deny the story which was carried in The Globe and Mail this morning.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Pontiac-Gatineau-Labelle (Mr. Lefebvre), for whom I have a great deal of respect, really answered the question himself as to why I sought out the Speaker. I tried to put that at the beginning of my argument. He said the government House leader has a responsible position in this House. That is exactly the reason. I think I said in the course of my argument that I have two responsibilities. As I view my responsibilities-there may be some disagreement with respect to this-I do take my responsibilities to the House of Commons quite seriously, and when a group of members of Parliament have some difficulty which I interpret as causing some difficulty in the operation of the business of the House of Commons, I think it is not improper for me to go to the Speaker of the House of Commons.
You may overrule me with respect to this, Mr. Speaker, and I will be prepared to abide by your ruling, but it has always been my understanding, and nothing has happened this afternoon to indicate that that understanding is wrong, that members of the House of Commons have a right to mention a concern to the Speaker. Members of the government have a right to mention concerns to the Speaker. Members of the opposition, their leader, have a right to mention concerns to the Speaker. What would be wrong would be a representation in the sense the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood (Mr. Rae) spoke of it.
I would take issue with him with respect not to his solution but with respect to his use of the word "representation". I think it is important when any member goes to see the Speaker for any reason at all that there should be no attempt by that member, whether he is a private member or a member of the government, to require an advance ruling or to preclude proper discussion of a point of order or to bring undue pressure on the Speaker. Mr. Speaker, you yourself have answered that argument today. You have indicated you were not influenced by what I said except that you decided to call a meeting at which the hon. member for Pontiac was there representing his party, my parliamentary secretary was there representing his party, and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) was there representing his party.
Let me just say with respect to the division of the parties in this House that the concern I expressed to you was sufficient for you to call a meeting of representatives of the parties. I regret I could not have been there, as 1 am sure the hon. member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso regrets he could not have been there. But all parties were ably represented. I think that is the position in which I find myself.
I want to say to hon. members that if I am seen speaking to Mr. Speaker in the hall-I say this through you, sir-it would be in that way that I would be speaking to Mr. Speaker. It would be on that assumption. I want to say to the hon. and reverend member for Eglinton-Lawrence (Mr. de Corneille) that that is exactly the way in which I have always approached my role. I think it is a responsible way to approach my role. I think it is a responsible way to approach my role.

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE

Just deny the story.
November 7, 1979

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext:
I have indicated that I am not responsible for the essence of timing in the story that might appear in The Globe and Mail or the Carp Review.
The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Reid) indicated that sometimes difficulties can occur. I might have been inarticulate in what 1 said. I may be at fault for what appears there by being inarticulate, and if that is the case I accept the responsibility. But the bottom line of all this is whether or not the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton, who happens to be the President of Privy Council and the leader of the government in the House of Commons, went to you, Mr. Speaker, and had the temerity even to think of influencing, let alone undertake the influencing, of the Speaker of the House of Commons. If I did that, I ought not to be a member of this place, and if you accepted it in that way, you ought not to be Speaker. Neither of those things occurred, and both you and I know it.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: I know the hon. member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) seeks to intervene because he was referred to earlier in the context of whether or not he would withdraw. We have had a long enough discussion, it seems to me, and I really wonder if there need be any more participation.

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Very briefly, Mr. Speaker. In his second intervention the President of Privy Council (Mr. Baker) mentioned that I had imputed motives and cast some doubt on Your Honour's integrity. I want to say clearly that my intervention had nothing to do with your conduct but rather it had to do with the conduct of the President of Privy Council himself. He has had three occasions this afternoon upon which to clearly express his point of view. I must say his third intervention was better than the second and much better than the first one, which was pretty shabby and very bad.
I want to assure you, Mr. Speaker, that in my intervention at that time I wanted clarification from the President of the Privy Council of what he said to The Globe and Mail. Quite clearly, we know what he told Your Honour. We know very well that Your Honour cannot be influenced, but we are still uncertain as to what the President of Privy Council said to The Globe and Mail and what he said to the representative of the Creditistes in this House. This is still in doubt, and my representation to Your Honour has been on that very point.

Mr. Speaker, I want to be very brief in my intervention. In my seven years here this is the first time I have witnessed a day such as this. Having worked under Your Honour for three years I seriously question the intervention of the President of Privy Council (Mr. Baker) on three occasions. His declaration to The Globe and Mail questions Your Honour's integrity. I feel
Privilege-Mr. Pinard
seriously about that, and I would very much like him to retract that. We have respect for the Chair, and I would like him to have that same respect.

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE

Mr. Speaker, I rise again only for a moment because my name was also mentioned by the President of Privy Council. He did so indirectly by reading an interesting article written by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Reid). In that article there are references to the many meetings the hon. member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso (Mr. MacEachen) and I had during the Parliament of 1972 to 1974. The President of Privy Council said we were both blushing. I think we probably blushed only because of the normal modesty of politicians when their names are mentioned.
However, I should like to assure the President of Privy Council and this House that far from being concerned about references to those meetings I am proud of those meetings and proud of what we won for the people of Canada because we held those meetings.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext:
I knew we would occasionally wander a little off the topic, but I did not think we were going to get back to the Parliament between 1972 and 1974 before we finished.
The questions raised by the hon. member for Drummond (Mr. Pinard) first of all and, in turn, by the hon. member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) and the hon. member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso (Mr. MacEachen)-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: I still have* a question of privilege to raise, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. PINARD-RIGHT OF SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext:
We have been dealing so far with the questions raised by the hon. member for Drummond and the hon. member for Papineau relating to an article which appeared in The Globe and Mail yesterday. The question raised by the hon. member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso does not touch upon The Globe and Mail itself. The matter raised is a matter which the House, of course, takes seriously. I also take it very seriously, and I think the House has had a very extensive discussion. Yet, perhaps because this is a minority Parliament, we can feel ourselves under an obligation to be extremely cautious about things of this sort.
Perhaps over five years as the Speaker dealing with members who now are party leaders in this House-although two of them have changed seats-because we came to know each other there would be a natural tendency toward informality in our discussions. That is only natural, and I think a trust and confidence was built up during that time which it is only natural for me and other members to rely upon and perhaps to take for granted. I am absolutely satisfied that what the President of Privy Council was doing on this occasion was speaking to me in a way he did many times as opposition House leader in the last Parliament.
I do not set aside lightly the points raised. They are very serious, and I know the hon. member takes it seriously when he

November 7, 1979
Privilege-Mr. Pinard
apologizes to the House. If in any way-even as I think the hon. member for Pontiac-Gatineau-Labelle (Mr. Lefebvre) said in his last intervention; I think he used the word "inadvertently in his suggestion on that day he had put me in an awkward position and in turn put the House in an awkward position, he again apologizes for that.
The hon. member for Papineau said that the third intervention by the President of Privy Council (Mr. Baker) was better than the first two. Perhaps, then, we can just concentrate on that one. The President of Privy Council, it seems to me, at least in that intervention-that is the one I remember best because it was the most recent-said first of all that if the quality of the report in The Globe and Mail is not what it should be, he accepts responsibility for that and lays the blame on his inadequate expression to the reporter. I am paraphrasing, but he accepts that.
Second, if his making a suggestion to me, which I subsequently discussed on that same day with representatives of all parties, was seen at any time as a representation which was improper in any way, he apologizes for that. If in the future conduct is such that we must be more scrupulous between the parties in that regard, which has been suggested-that is to say, all members and the Chair-it is something which I think all members would regret.
I think it again indicates to us that in a minority situation where the representations are so close and the situation so fragile perhaps we do have to be a little more formal, a little more careful, exercise more caution and perhaps less friendliness and informality. I hope that is not the case, but in any event I accept-as I am sure the House does-the intervention of the President of Privy Council, who says he intended no such influence, would never dream that such would be taken by me in that context, and that he had only the intention of making a suggestion knowing it would be discussed at a meeting later that day which in fact took place and at which all parties were represented. I and I am sure the House accept that. Perhaps, however, the one benefit from this discussion is that we are cautioned to be extremely careful about all these matters.
I close finally by returning to the point of the hon. member for Drummond who raised, I thought and as I indicated earlier, a very valid point relating to the use of Standing Order 29. For the benefit of those who are puzzled by the application I made of it yesterday, I can indicate that it is my understanding that when the Chair makes a selection as envisaged by that rule, a member can only seek the floor to question that by putting, on a point of order, the motion which is contained in Standing Order 29.
I have given the hon. member my reasons for not allowing him to do that yesterday. I was attempting to settle a problem which had been outstanding in the House for quite some time, so I was more than just recognizing a member for debate; I was also deciding a procedural point which I thought ought not to be the subject of appeal by the House at that time. These two rules came in conflict, and I had to decide rather quickly how to apply them, and 1 did; but I think the hon.

member might be comforted by knowing that if in future he wishes to take advantage of Standing Order 29, he should do it in exactly the way he tried to do it yesterday.
I might also point out in conclusion-and I thought I should put the substantive matters forward first-that since by neither motion am I asked to take any particular action on procedural grounds-I have no motion before me to consider, in other words-I therefore set aside the questions of privilege on the dispositions I have just made.
MR. MacEACHEN-ENERGY SUPPLIES ALLOCATION BOARD-

subtopic: ANSWERS OF MINISTER OF ENERGY, MINES AND RESOURCES

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Cape Breton Highlands-Canso):
speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: ANSWERS OF MINISTER OF ENERGY, MINES AND RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think this is the first time I have ever raised a question of privilege in the House of Commons. If that is not correct, then it is one of the few times.
My question of privilege has to do with the events which took place in the House of Commons yesterday, but in a sense it is not unrelated to the discussion we had earlier. I have no desire to reopen that discussion, although I am tempted to say that a certain benefit has been developed, because in referring to the co-operation which the President of Privy Council (Mr. Baker) alleged existed between the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and myself, he obviously made a declaration of a very close and co-operative arrangement between his party and the Social Credit group.
On the same subject I say to my friend, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, that obviously the influence of that contact with the government which he had in those years of great progress, as he said, has not really left him because he sounded very much today like a member of a government party rather than a member of the opposition, which is his normal role.
I intend to be brief and to the point. Yesterday in the House of Commons I clearly asked the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Hnatyshyn) the question whether he would move to establish with some speed the Emergency Supplies Allocation Board. I asked him to justify why he had not appointed members of the board, and if he had not done so to date, why would he not do it at that very moment and announce it to the House. Later the hon. member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. McRae) asked the same question.
In reply to both of these questions the hon. minister clearly and certainly misled me. The only reasonable conclusion which can be drawn from his answers was that he had not moved, and was not intending at that time to move, to establish the membership of the board. He said to me that I did not understand the situation because "the fact of the matter is that the department is setting up a support basis upon which any emergency allocation would be available". He went on to say that if a crisis occurred, which he did not think existed, then he might move to establish the Emergency Supplies Allocation Board.
November 7, 1979

I accepted the minister's answers. I went to a meeting and at about 5.30 or six o'clock I received a message that the Canadian Press had put on the wire a news report that the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) stated Tuesday that the government will establish an Energy Supplies Allocation Board which, under existing legislation, would have the power to impose petroleum rationing.
I asked the minister between two and three o'clock, and at five o'clock or thereabouts, the Canadian Press was told. Then it was disclosed in the House that the Prime Minister had written a letter to the leader of the Social Credit group. In that letter he told him the following:
In this connection, you may have noted that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has indicated his intention to seek some administrative changes to the Energy Supplies Emergency Act and at the same time announce appointment of an Energy Supplies Allocation Board.
That is a letter from the Prime Minister to the leader of the Social Credit group. It was tabled by the Prime Minister some time before the adjournment at six o'clock.

subtopic: ANSWERS OF MINISTER OF ENERGY, MINES AND RESOURCES

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: ANSWERS OF MINISTER OF ENERGY, MINES AND RESOURCES
speechtext:
At 5.25 p.m. I asked the question, the hon. member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan asked the question, and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources just concealed the information from us. I have a tendency to believe that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources did not know what was in the Prime Minister's letter. If that is the explanation, I hold him free and uncriticized. But if he knew the information at that time, then it was his duty to let it be known to the House of Commons. The open government policy has proclaimed respect for Parliament, but it was totally ignored in this case.
Further I must say I am astonished that the Prime Minister, who obviously had written the letter or was writing the letter to the leader of the Social Credit group, and who was listening to my questions to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, did not send him a note and say, "Minister, bear in mind I am notifiyng the leader of the Social Credit party that we are going to do that". It all fits together very nicely. I was denied the information, the House was denied the information, but it was conveyed in a private arrangement to the Social Credit group by a letter from the Prime Minister, so that the government would get some points and some support, presumably, that evening from the Social Credit group.
I object very strongly, but I withhold further comment because I realize the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and the Prime Minister are not in their places.
I lay the foundation for raising the matter when the minister is in his place, because he had the nerve and the audacity to say in his speech after eight o'clock that he had announced already in the House the information about the establishment of the Emergency Supplies Allocation Board. This is very serious, and I want to indicate to the minister that if he does not have a pretty good explanation for the House, then certainly we will have reason to change our attitude to him and to
Privilege-Mr. MacEachen
what he tells us in reply to questions in the House of Commons.

Thank you for the promotion, Mr. Speaker. I wish to know if you could give me some explanation on a very important point. The right hon. speechtext: Excuse me, hon. members opposite did it often, if they do not mind. They are silent now that they are sitting over there. After receiving unanimous consent of the House yesterday, could somebody please tell us why it was not done then?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ANSWERS OF MINISTER OF ENERGY, MINES AND RESOURCES
speechtext: Perhaps it relates to the earlier intervention of the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) when he was asked if he could table the letters. He said at the time that he did not have the English version of the letter from the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Roy), that he had his own and that he was prepared to table it. Also he indicated that if we could get the letter from the hon. member for Beauce later, it would be tabled as well. Simply there may have been some confusion. It was not clear whether the undertaking of the Prime Minister was to table one or two letters. In any case I think it was the consensus of the House that both letters should be tabled, and I believe the offer of the President of Privy Council and Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Baker) was to complete that. One letter has, of course, been appended to Hansard as tabled yesterday.

subtopic: ANSWERS OF MINISTER OF ENERGY, MINES AND RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 think it is exactly on the same point. In my opinion the mistake which may have been committed yesterday should not have happened if one carefully reads Hansard and the speeches made by hon. members who took part in this exchange between on the one hand the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Roy) and on the other hand the hon. member for Pontiac-Gatineau-Labelle (Mr. Lefebvre), the member for Saguenay and others.
It is quite clear that we want the whole correspondence and not just the French and English copies of the letter written by the Prime Minister to the hon. member for Beauce. To understand better the debate, we certainly want to see the letter written by the hon. member for Beauce to the Prime Minister. If we really want to understand what actually happened we must be able to read what the hon. member for Beauce, the hon. leader of the Social Credit Party of Canada, wanted to ask the Prime Minister for him to take time to answer it. In any case, the Prime Minister's reply is quite clear to us because he recognizes-and that to us is very important-if you read that letter very carefully that:
[English)
Should we be faced with a disruption of oil supply sufficient to cause a national emergency, then I can assure you that the government is prepared to use the powers available to it under the Energy Supplies Emergency Act, 1979, to conserve supplies-


So this is very important to us because this answer from the Prime Minister is quite revealing of the new intentions of the government which is now prepared to use legislation passed by the former government. Indeed we would like to know what the hon. member for Beauce asked the Prime Minister that justified such an interesting answer for those who follow the debates closely. I think our hon. friend is probably right when he says that it must have gone unnoticed. However, it did not go unnoticed to us since we are trying to find out what the hon. member for Beauce could have asked the Prime Minister to receive such an extraordinary complete answer and so quickly, the very same afternoon, of course, of a debate which ended in a very important vote last night.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ANSWERS OF MINISTER OF ENERGY, MINES AND RESOURCES
speechtext: Again I say the simple answer is that the conversation at one time would indicate that the Prime Minister was only tabling his letter because that is all he had, and subsequently the other letter was not available.

In order to clarify the situation, as we went through this a few days ago, this is correspondence. It was written originally, in this case, in the French language by the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Roy) because that is the language he chooses to operate in, and it will not be translated by the House unless the House now orders that this be done when it is tabled and appended to Hansard as if it had been read as part of the record. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret having to raise this point of order so late in the afternoon, but as you are aware this is the only time I can raise a point of order in connection with the production of papers. On October 31 the Parliamentary Secretary to President of Privy Council (Mr. Kilgour), as it is reported in Hansard at page 810, said:
-notices of motions for the production of papers Nos. 29 and 31 are acceptable to the government.
On page 811, the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) is reported as saying:
-I rise on a point of order. I hope it has not escaped the attention of the House that when the first four motions for the production of papers were called, the motions were granted.
My point of order is in two parts. The first part deals with my motion No. 29 and motion 31, which belongs to the hon. member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson). As of this day these papers have not been tabled. Under the rules, there appears to be no time limit for the production of papers. My point is that I am somewhat confused about the agreement because there has been an apparent agreement to table papers and, therefore, the motion is removed from the order paper as though the papers have been produced.
I can understand a delay of one, two or three days, but it seemed at the time it was agreed that the papers would be produced or that the papers had been found and were therefore readily available. Is there any limit as to the time the government can take to produce these papers? That is my first point.
My second point also deals with the production of papers on that same day. The Parliamentary Secretary to President of Privy Council said at page 810 of Hansard:
Notices of motions for the production of papers Nos. 18 and 23 are acceptable to the government subject to the authorization of the government of Quebec.
The first motion deals with flooding in the Lake of Two Mountains area, and the second with the public transportation situation in Montreal west. The assumption is that when the province of Quebec gives agreement, then these papers will be produced. My difficulty, first of all, is that I have no idea if the government has contacted the government of the province of Quebec to inquire whether it is possible that they may give their agreement to release these documents. Or alternatively, if the government knows that the government of the province of Quebec will not agree to the production of these documents, the government is able, under the guise of producing papers, to make this statement in the House which leaves me to believe that at some future date I may receive these documents.
My last point is that I would assume from what I learned on October 31 that the government will make some effort to see whether it is possible for those papers to be produced. I therefore wonder if any effort has been made on their part, whether it be by phone call, letter or whatever, that at some date in the future-hopefully not too long-there will be a statement from the government of the province of Quebec that they agree to the production of these papers or, to the con-
November 7, 1979

trary, they do not agree, at which point in time I will then be able to continue with any arguments on which I wish to proceed in this House.
There are two points I am making. The first concerns the documents which the government agreed to produce and on which there appears to be no time limit. The second is that the government says "subject to the actions of someone else", without indicating whether they intend to pursue the matter or whether even, in my capacity as the hon. member for Vau-dreuil, I must now contact the government of the province of Quebec to see if I can get a release of the documents which I require.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to associate myself briefly with the comments made by the hon. member for Vaudreuil and to point out the difficulty in which members are placed. When the government says that it has no objection to giving us papers, the order for the motion to produce papers is struck from the record, but then in fact the papers are not produced. My staff has made innumerable telephone calls without any success.
The motion which I put was a very simple one. I asked for all the form letters which are now being used in connection with establishing relationships in the case of sponsored relatives in Southeast Asia. It is a matter of importance to the people of Toronto. It is a contentious issue on which we hear a lot of different opinions, and having those forms to examine would assist my work.
The government has said that it is willing to produce the forms, and yet a week later, apparently, there is no hope in sight of my getting them. My concern is that the motion has now been stricken, and this gives the impression that my request has been granted when it has not. I am sure that there is no deliberate intent to obstruct, but in raising this matter I hope that a solution will be found.

speechtext:
The population of certain areas of Canada, especially the eastern region, that is Quebec and the maritimes, is seriously concerned about the security of gasoline and heating oil supplies next winter.
It is therefore vitally important that your government announce immediately to the population of Canada what action
it has already taken or intends to take and what guarantees it can give to avoid any possibility of a shortage which could cause panic and eventually lead to an excessive price increase.
Moreover, it is also extremely important that all necessary action be taken to protect and guarantee the quotas of independent distributors.
I therefore hope for a quick reply, in the form, for instance, of a ministerial statement.
Sincerely yours,
Fabien Roy
c.c. Hon. Ray Hnatyshyn Hon. Walter Baker
